body:
1. What Is a Cell?

Every living organism, from a microscopic bacterium to a large tree or human being, is made up of cells. A cell is the smallest basic structural and functional unit of a living organism. It is called a structural unit because cells form the bodies of organisms. It is called a functional unit because living cells perform essential activities such as obtaining nutrients, releasing energy, eliminating waste, growing and responding to their surroundings.

Cell: The basic structural and functional unit of life, capable of carrying out essential life processes.

A cell is not simply a small compartment. It is an organised living system containing substances and structures that work together. Some organisms consist of only 1 cell, while others consist of many specialised cells.

2. Discovery of Cells and Development of Cell Theory

The discovery of cells became possible after the development of microscopes. Several scientists contributed to the understanding that cells form the basic organisation of living organisms.

  • Robert Hooke (1665): Examined a thin slice of cork using a microscope and observed numerous small compartments resembling a honeycomb. He named them cells. The compartments were the walls of dead cork cells, not living cells.
  • Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (1674): Observed free-living microscopic organisms in pond water using improved microscopes.
  • Robert Brown (1831): Identified the nucleus in plant cells.
  • Matthias Schleiden (1838): Concluded that plants are composed of cells.
  • Theodor Schwann (1839): Extended the cellular understanding to animals and helped formulate cell theory.
  • Rudolf Virchow (1855): Established the principle that new cells arise from pre-existing cells.

The 3 Principles of Cell Theory

Cell theory explains the cellular organisation and continuity of life. Its 3 classical principles are:

  1. All living organisms are composed of 1 or more cells.
  2. The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
  3. New cells arise from pre-existing cells through cell division.

These principles connect the structure of an organism with its growth and reproduction. A multicellular organism develops through repeated cell divisions, and its cells become specialised to perform different functions.

Cell theory concerns cellular life. Viruses are acellular infectious agents. They do not possess normal cellular organisation and depend on living host cells for multiplication. They should not be confused with unicellular organisms.

3. Unicellular and Multicellular Organisms

Unicellular Organisms

A unicellular organism consists of a single cell that performs all essential life functions. Examples include bacteria, Amoeba, Paramecium and many unicellular algae.

Amoeba obtains food, exchanges gases, removes wastes and moves using its single cell. It forms temporary extensions called pseudopodia, or false feet, for movement and food capture.

Multicellular Organisms

A multicellular organism contains many cells, often specialised for particular functions. For example, muscle cells produce movement, nerve cells transmit signals, and blood cells perform transport or defence functions.

This specialisation is called division of labour. Groups of cooperating cells form tissues, different tissues form organs, and organs work together in organ systems.

For example, muscle tissue and nervous tissue contribute to the functioning of the stomach. Similarly, different tissues in a plant stem provide support and transport substances.

4. Variation in Cell Shape and Size

Cells differ in shape and size because their structures are adapted to their functions. Most cells are microscopic, although some egg cells are large enough to be seen without a microscope.

  • Amoeba: Has a changing shape because it forms pseudopodia.
  • Nerve cell: Has a cell body and long processes that help transmit information over distances.
  • Muscle cell: Has an elongated form suited to contraction.
  • Red blood cell: In humans, has a biconcave shape that provides a large surface area for gas exchange.
  • Ostrich egg: Is a familiar example of a very large single cell.

A larger organism does not necessarily have larger individual cells. An elephant is much larger than a rat mainly because of differences in the total number and organisation of cells, not because every elephant cell is proportionately larger.

Prelims focus

  • Robert Hooke first described cells in cork in 1665.
  • Schleiden (1838) studied plant cells; Schwann (1839) extended cell theory to animals.
  • Virchow (1855) established that cells arise from pre-existing cells.
  • Amoeba is unicellular; a human being is multicellular.
  • Cell shape is related to function, and body size does not directly determine cell size.
  • Trap: Hooke observed the walls of dead cork cells, not living cells.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 8, Cell—Structure and Functions, pp. 90–94; NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 5, The Fundamental Unit of Life, pp. 57–59; NCERT, Exploration, Class 9, Chapter 2, Cell: The Building Block of Life, Section 2.5, online text consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Cells: The Fundamental Structural and Functional Units of Life

body:
1. Basic Organisation of a Cell

Most cells contain a boundary called the plasma membrane, an internal region called the cytoplasm, and genetic material containing hereditary information. Cells differ in how these components are organised.

The plasma membrane separates the internal contents from the surrounding environment. The cytoplasm contains fluid and cellular structures in which numerous activities occur. Genetic material provides information necessary for cellular organisation and continuity.

Cells are broadly classified as prokaryotic or eukaryotic according to the organisation of their genetic material and internal structures.

2. Prokaryotic Cells

Prokaryotic cells do not have a well-defined nucleus surrounded by a nuclear membrane. Their principal genetic material occupies a region called the nucleoid.

They also lack membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, Golgi apparatus and endoplasmic reticulum. However, they possess ribosomes, which make proteins. Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller and structurally simpler than typical eukaryotic cells.

Examples: Bacteria and cyanobacteria, traditionally called blue-green algae.

Many bacterial cells possess a cell wall outside the plasma membrane. Their cell walls should not be assumed to have the same composition as the cellulose-based walls of plants.

3. Eukaryotic Cells

Eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus in which genetic material is enclosed by a nuclear membrane. They also contain several membrane-bound organelles that perform specialised functions.

Eukaryotic organisms include plants, animals, fungi and protists such as Amoeba and Paramecium. A eukaryotic organism may be unicellular or multicellular.

FeatureProkaryotic cellEukaryotic cell
NucleusNo membrane-bound nucleusMembrane-bound nucleus present
Genetic materialPrincipal DNA in nucleoidChromosomes inside nucleus
Membrane-bound organellesAbsentPresent
RibosomesPresentPresent
Typical sizeGenerally smallerGenerally larger
ExamplesBacteria, cyanobacteriaPlants, animals, Amoeba

Unicellular is not the same as prokaryotic. A bacterium is unicellular and prokaryotic, whereas Amoeba is unicellular and eukaryotic.

4. Plant Cells and Animal Cells

Plant and animal cells are both eukaryotic. They possess a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and several common organelles. Their differences arise mainly from the requirements of their way of life.

Cell Wall

Most plant cells have a rigid cell wall outside the plasma membrane. It is composed mainly of cellulose and provides support, protection and resistance against excessive swelling.

Animal cells lack a cell wall. Their plasma membrane forms the outer cellular boundary, allowing greater flexibility of shape.

Plastids

Plant cells may contain plastids. The best-known example is the chloroplast, which contains chlorophyll and carries out photosynthesis.

Animal cells do not possess plastids. However, not every plant cell contains chloroplasts. For example, ordinary underground root cells generally lack chloroplasts because they do not normally perform photosynthesis.

Vacuoles

Many mature plant cells contain a large central vacuole filled with cell sap. It stores substances and helps maintain the pressure that keeps the cell firm.

Animal cells may contain smaller vacuoles or vesicles, but they generally do not have the same large central vacuole typical of mature plant cells.

5. Important Qualifications

Biological classifications describe typical structures, but specialised cells can differ. For example, mature human red blood cells lack a nucleus, although they are animal cells. This does not make them prokaryotic: they develop from eukaryotic cells and are specialised for oxygen transport.

Similarly, a cell wall is not exclusive to plants. Bacteria and fungi also possess cell walls, although their wall materials differ.

Prelims focus

  • The nucleoid is associated with prokaryotic cells.
  • A membrane-bound nucleus is characteristic of eukaryotic cells.
  • Ribosomes occur in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
  • A typical plant cell has a cellulose cell wall; an animal cell does not.
  • Chloroplasts perform photosynthesis; large plant vacuoles maintain turgidity.
  • Trap: Amoeba is unicellular but eukaryotic, and mature human red blood cells lack nuclei.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 8, pp. 93–97; NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 5, pp. 61–65; GCERT, Science, Standard 9, Chapter 5, The Fundamental Unit of Life, pp. 53–57; NCERT, Exploration, Class 9, Chapter 2, Sections 2.2–2.3, online text consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Labelled bacterial, plant and animal cells compare an unenclosed DNA nucleoid with membrane-bound nuclei and show their main structures.
pictures.caption: Structural organisation of a bacterial cell, a typical plant cell and a typical animal cell.

title: Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic Cells: Structure and Differences

body:
1. The Plasma Membrane Controls Exchange

The plasma membrane, also called the cell membrane, separates the interior of a cell from its environment. It consists mainly of lipids and proteins and is flexible rather than rigid.

The membrane is described as selectively permeable because it permits some substances to cross while restricting others. The movement of materials across this boundary allows cells to obtain necessary substances and eliminate wastes.

Two important school-level processes involved in movement are diffusion and osmosis.

2. Diffusion: Movement Down a Concentration Difference

Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration because of their random motion.

Diffusion can occur in gases and liquids and does not inherently require a membrane. When a concentration difference exists, particles move randomly in both directions, but the overall movement is towards the region of lower concentration.

For example, carbon dioxide produced during cellular respiration may accumulate inside a cell. If its concentration is higher inside than outside, carbon dioxide diffuses outward. Oxygen can diffuse into a cell when its concentration is higher outside than inside.

Diffusion helps explain the exchange of gases between cells and their surroundings. The direction of net movement depends on the concentration difference, not simply on whether a substance is useful or harmful to the cell.

3. Osmosis: Movement of Water Through a Selectively Permeable Membrane

Osmosis is the net movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane from a region of higher water concentration to a region of lower water concentration.

In ordinary dilute solutions, the region with fewer dissolved particles has a higher concentration of water. Consequently, water generally moves towards the side with more dissolved solute, provided the membrane allows water to cross and the relevant solute is restricted.

Osmosis is a special case of diffusion involving water and a selectively permeable membrane. It is important in water absorption by living root cells and in maintaining cell volume.

FeatureDiffusionOsmosis
Substances movingParticles such as gases or dissolved substancesWater
Membrane requirementNot necessarily requiredSelectively permeable membrane required
Net directionHigher to lower concentration of moving substanceHigher to lower water concentration
Cell exampleOxygen and carbon dioxide exchangeWater entering or leaving cells

4. Effects of Different Solutions on Cells

When a cell is placed in a solution, its response depends on the relative concentration of dissolved substances inside and outside the cell.

Hypotonic Solution

A solution is hypotonic relative to a cell when its effective solute concentration is lower than that of the cell contents. Water enters the cell by osmosis, causing it to swell.

A plant cell becomes firm or turgid because the cell wall resists excessive expansion. An animal cell, which lacks a rigid cell wall, may swell greatly and can burst under sufficiently extreme conditions.

Isotonic Solution

A solution is isotonic when there is no net osmotic movement of water across the cell membrane. Water molecules continue moving in both directions, but the opposing movements balance one another.

An animal cell generally maintains its normal volume in an isotonic solution. A plant cell in such a solution does not develop the high turgor characteristic of a well-watered cell.

Hypertonic Solution

A solution is hypertonic relative to a cell when its effective solute concentration is greater than that of the cell contents. Water moves out of the cell by osmosis.

An animal cell shrinks. In a plant cell, loss of water reduces pressure against the cell wall. With sufficient water loss, the plasma membrane and living contents pull away from the wall, producing plasmolysis.

5. Everyday Applications of Osmosis

When dried raisins are placed in water, they absorb water and swell. In a sufficiently concentrated sugar solution, they lose water and shrink. These observations illustrate the effect of relative solute concentration on water movement.

Salting freshly cut vegetables provides another familiar example. Salt increases the dissolved solute concentration around exposed cells, encouraging water to leave them. As the cells lose water and turgidity, the vegetable may become limp.

Plasmolysis and the Cell Wall

In a living plant cell placed in a sufficiently hypertonic solution, the plasma membrane may pull away from the cell wall as the cell loses water. The rigid cell wall largely retains its original shape while the living contents contract.

This demonstrates that the cell wall and plasma membrane are distinct structures. The cell wall provides mechanical support, while the plasma membrane controls the movement of many substances.

No net movement does not mean no movement. In an isotonic solution, water crosses the membrane in both directions. The overall transfer is zero because the opposing movements balance.

6. The Importance of Cell Water Balance

Osmosis contributes to the firmness of leaves and young stems, water uptake by plant cells and maintenance of cellular volume. When plant cells lose substantial water, leaves and soft shoots may wilt because their cells lose turgor.

Water movement is therefore directly connected to cellular structure and to the visible condition of whole plant tissues.

Prelims focus

  • The plasma membrane is selectively permeable and consists mainly of lipids and proteins.
  • Diffusion is net movement from higher to lower concentration of the moving particles.
  • Osmosis involves water movement through a selectively permeable membrane.
  • Hypotonic surroundings generally cause water entry; hypertonic surroundings cause water loss.
  • Plasmolysis involves separation of the living cell contents from the plant cell wall after sufficient water loss.
  • Trap: A plant cell wall is not the same as the selectively permeable plasma membrane.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 5, Sections 5.2.1–5.2.2, pp. 59–61; GCERT, Science, Standard 9, Chapter 5, pp. 51–53; NCERT, Exploration, Class 9, Chapter 2, Section 2.2, online text consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Water movement and cell behaviour in hypotonic, isotonic and hypertonic solutions.

title: Plasma Membrane, Diffusion, Osmosis and Cell Water Balance
